citation.title: On the reliability of published findings using the regression discontinuity design in political science

standing_assumptions:
The article (Research and Politics, April–June 2023, pp. 1–12; printed page numbers equal PDF page numbers) is a survey and reanalysis of 45 published regression discontinuity (RD) studies. It states no theorem, proposition, lemma or proof and displays no formula; its mathematical content is in running text, in Tables 1–3 and in Figures 1–5. Every passage of the article quoted in this file was read from the page images. The official online supplement (Sections S1–S9, 23 pp.) is staged only as a text extraction, with no rendered pages; the few supplement passages quoted here (Section S4, Section S9, Figure S9) are transcribed from that extraction and are marked as such wherever they occur.
(S1) Estimand and identification. p. 3 (PDF p. 3), section ‘Why is it hard to estimate RD effects?’: “The causal effect studied in the RD design is the difference between the expected treated and control potential outcomes at a cutoff where treatment assignment changes in a discontinuous fashion. If the conditional expectation function of the outcome were known, this effect can be calculated without error under an assumption that the conditional expectation functions of the potential outcomes are continuous at the cut point. In other words, the RD effect is identified under a continuity assumption.” The paper uses no symbols for these objects. The targets write $X$ for the running variable, $c$ for the cutoff, $Y(1)$ and $Y(0)$ for the potential outcomes, $D = \mathbf{1}\{X \ge c\}$ for treatment in a sharp design, and $\tau = E[Y(1)\mid X = c] - E[Y(0)\mid X = c]$ for the RD effect, with both conditional expectation functions continuous at $c$.
(S2) Estimation. p. 3 (PDF p. 3): “The standard way to proceed is to assume that the potential outcome functions are smooth, meaning that they do not change too quickly. This implies that observations close to the cutoff are somewhat informative of the value of the functions at the cutoff, so they can be used for estimation.” and “We can interpret this as a bias–variance trade-off, where the bias is governed by the relevance of the observations and the variance by their numbers.” No smoothness class, bound or rate is stated.
(S3) Inference. p. 3 (PDF p. 3): “To conduct hypothesis tests or construct confidence intervals, researchers need to estimate the accuracy of the RD point estimate. Conventional methods used to gauge this accuracy rely on an assumption that the bias of the estimator is negligible compared to its variance, as would be the case in, for example, a randomized experiment. However, when a bandwidth selection method balances bias and variance to maximize accuracy, the bias is not negligible, and it must therefore be accounted for when drawing inference. Researchers sometimes neglect doing so, with the consequence that their hypothesis tests and confidence intervals are misleading even when the sample is large.” The three remedies the paper recognizes, pp. 3–4 (PDF pp. 3–4): “The first approach is so-called undersmoothing, meaning that one uses a bandwidth that is smaller than the optimal one. If done correctly, this will ensure that the bias indeed is negligible in large samples, so researchers can use conventional methods to construct hypothesis tests and confidence intervals.”; “The second approach is to adjust the inference procedure for the bias. […] The alternative approach described by Calonico et al. (2014), which is becoming the standard approach used in political science, is to also estimate the precision of the bias adjustment and incorporate this into the variance estimator. This allows researchers to use bias adjustments that have similar precision as the point estimator (e.g., as would be the case when the same bandwidth is used for both point and bias estimation), and it should improve finite sample performance.”; “The third approach is to adjust the inference procedure with the worse-case bias consistent with the observed data. The worst-case is taken with respect to a stipulated class of functions, in which the true conditional expectation function is assumed to exist.”
(S4) Sample and $t$-statistics. p. 4 (PDF p. 4): “There were 45 studies in total that satisfied these inclusion criteria.” and “Figure 1 presents the distribution of $t$-statistics for the published findings among all 45 studies in our sample. The first panel presents the distribution of the main reported result of each article, meaning that each article contributes one $t$-statistic. The second panel presents the distribution of all results that were referenced in the articles’ abstracts, which we take as a proxy for being a primary result of an article. There are 80 $t$-statistics in total in the second panel, meaning that each article contributes 1.78 statistics on average. To avoid overrepresentation of articles that present many results, the $t$-statistics in the second panel are weighted by the inverse of the total number of results in each study. For the majority of the studies, we either use reported $t$-statistics or reconstruct $t$-statistics using the ratio of coefficients and standard errors. For the small number of the studies where neither $t$-statistics nor standard errors were reported, we reconstruct $t$-statistics using reported $p$-values, confidence intervals and point estimates, or using replication code and data provided by the authors.” The horizontal axis of the histograms is labelled ‘t−statistic’, with ticks 0.98, 1.96, 2.94, 3.92; that the plotted and tested statistics are absolute values is read from the replication code, not from the text.
(S5) Reanalysis. p. 7 (PDF p. 7), Methodology: “We were able to obtain such data for 36 out of the 45 studies in our sample.”; “Our primary reanalysis uses the default settings in the R package rdrobust (Calonico et al., 2015). The procedure implemented in this package has well-understood theoretical properties and attempts to address the concerns discussed in the \emph{Why is it hard to estimate RD effects?} section. The reanalysis results we present in the main body of the paper exclude all studies that originally used the rdrobust package to estimate the effects, as a reanalysis would bring few new insights for these studies. This results in 39 estimates across 25 studies.”; “One limitation of the approach by Calonico et al. (2015) is that it is motivated by an asymptotic approximation. This means that confidence intervals and hypothesis tests may not be valid in finite samples.” The three panels of Figures 3 and 4 (p. 7, Results) are: the original analyses; “the default bandwidth selection method implemented in rdrobust (“mserd”)” with no “adjustments for bias for the point estimator nor any adjustments for the standard errors”; and the same bandwidth selection with “the bias adjustment for the point estimator” and estimated standard errors adjusted “to account for the added imprecision of the bias adjustment”.
(S6) Power analysis. p. 9 (PDF p. 9): “To investigate the extent to which this is a relevant concern among RD studies in political science, we conducted retrospective power analyses for all 36 studies with replication data, comprising 64 separate analyses. Using the power analysis method implemented in the R package rdpower by Cattaneo et al. (2019), we estimate the power of a two-tailed test at the 5% significance level based on a central limit approximation for the sampling distribution. The power analyses presume that $p$-values will be constructed with the bias adjustment and robust standard errors as implemented by rdrobust. As this procedure is only asymptotically valid, our power calculations may be optimistic relative to approaches that control the false positive rate in finite samples.”; “We measure effect size by Cohen’s $d$, which is the treatment effect standardized by the standard deviation of the outcome (Cohen, 1988). We use the standard deviation of the outcome of control units within the default bandwidth in the rdrobust package for this standardization. We investigate the effect sizes 0.1, 0.2, 0.5 and 0.8.”; “Table 2 presents the results from the power analyses. The cells give the proportion of the 64 analyses that attain the power specified by the columns for the effect size specified by the rows. For example, we see that only 17% of the analyses attain 60% power to detect a standardized effect of 0.1. We weigh the analyses in the same way as in Figure 1(b) to account for the fact that some studies conducted more analyses than others.”
(S7) Notation of the targets that is not in the paper. $\Phi$ and $\varphi$ are the distribution function and density of $N(0,1)$. $z = \Phi^{-1}(39/40)$ is the two-sided 5% normal critical value; the paper prints its rounding $1.96 = 49/25$ and the replication code uses the unrounded quantile ($1.95996398454000 < z < 1.95996398454010$). The normal-approximation power of the two-tailed 5% test of (S6), for a statistic distributed $N(\tau/s, 1)$ with $s > 0$, is $f(|\tau|/s)$ with $$f(a) = \Phi(a - z) + \Phi(-a - z), \qquad a \ge 0 .$$ For integers $0 \le k \le n$ and $p \in [0,1]$, $G_{n,k}(p) = \sum_{j=k}^{n} \binom{n}{j} p^j (1-p)^{n-j}$ is the upper tail of the Binomial$(n,p)$ distribution. Where a target takes a number from the deposited replication files (a stored standard error, a count, a weight), it says so and treats the number as a premise; such premises are not part of the mathematics to be proved.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: The Cohen's d standardization of p. 9 as applied to Coppock and Green (2016), and the cells of Tables 2 and 3 that depend on it, as repaired by Sol: an effect on a binary individual outcome is standardized by a standard deviation that is at most 1/2, so the study cannot reach 95% power at d = 0.1 (formal content: the bound on a binary standard deviation, the power bound, the one-row table arithmetic, and the invariance of the t-ratio)
canonical_claim.location: p. 9 (PDF p. 9), Power analysis and Table 2 (row 0.1, column 95); Table 3, p. 10 (PDF p. 10), ‘Studies not using election data’ (row 0.1, column 95)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed; p. 9] “We measure effect size by Cohen’s $d$, which is the treatment effect standardized by the standard deviation of the outcome (Cohen, 1988). We use the standard deviation of the outcome of control units within the default bandwidth in the rdrobust package for this standardization.” [Printed; Table 2, p. 9, row 0.1, column 95] 0.10. [Printed; Table 3, p. 10, ‘Studies not using election data’, row 0.1, columns 60 | 80 | 95] 0.40 | 0.35 | 0.28.
[Corrected; Sol's smallest_repair (validated.json, P033-N010), verbatim] “Use an individual baseline/control turnout SD in the intended local population, account for instrument orientation, and recompute this study’s power targets and standardized plot coordinates. Until that SD is available, mark its Cohen-d comparisons unavailable and qualify the affected summary entries; changing cutoff side alone is insufficient.”
[Mathematical content, with every hypothesis]
(i) [The standard deviation of a binary outcome] If $Y$ takes values in $\{0,1\}$ with $P(Y = 1) = p$, then $\mathrm{Var}(Y) = p(1-p) = \tfrac14 - (p - \tfrac12)^2 \le \tfrac14$, so $\mathrm{SD}(Y) \le \tfrac12$. For a sample of $N \ge 2$ binary values with mean $\hat p$, the sample variance with divisor $N - 1$ is $\tfrac{N}{N-1}\hat p(1 - \hat p) \le \tfrac{N}{4(N-1)}$. Hence an effect of $d = 0.1$ standard deviations of a binary individual outcome satisfies $|\tau| = 0.1\,\mathrm{SD} \le \tfrac{1}{20}$ in the population, and $|\tau| \le \tfrac{1}{20}\sqrt{N/(N-1)}$ with a sample standard deviation. The effect implied by the count standardization, $2.458$, is not a possible difference of two probabilities, which is at most $1$ in absolute value.
(ii) [The power function is increasing] With $z = \Phi^{-1}(39/40)$ and $f(a) = \Phi(a - z) + \Phi(-a - z)$: $f(0) = \tfrac{1}{20}$, $f'(a) = \varphi(a - z) - \varphi(a + z) > 0$ for $a > 0$, so $f$ is strictly increasing on $[0, \infty)$; and $f(a) < \Phi(a - z) + \tfrac{1}{40}$ for $a > 0$.
(iii) [The bound for this study] Premise from the deposited results: the stored bias-corrected robust standard error is $s = 0.0154987506828555$. For every $|\tau| \le \tfrac{1}{20}$, the normal-approximation power of (S6) satisfies $$f(|\tau|/s) \le f\big(\tfrac{1}{20 s}\big), \qquad 0.8972619 < f\big(\tfrac{1}{20 s}\big) < 0.8972620, \qquad\text{in particular } f(|\tau|/s) < \tfrac{19}{20},$$ where $\tfrac{1}{20s} = 3.2260664\ldots$ and $\tfrac{1}{20s} - z = 1.2661024\ldots$. Equivalently, the standard deviation $\sigma$ for which $f(0.1\,\sigma/s)$ equals $0.60$, $0.80$ and $0.95$ is $0.3430295\ldots$, $0.4342101\ldots$ and $0.5587016\ldots$ respectively, and the last exceeds $\tfrac12$. With the sample bound of (i) and $N \ge 31731$ (the validator's lower bound for the number of individuals in the local control pool) the standard deviation is at most $0.5000079$ and the power at most $0.8972711 < \tfrac{19}{20}$.
(iv) [The one-row change of the tables; premises from the deposited results] Premises: the study has weight $1$ and is a non-election study; the total weights are $36$ (Table 2) and $10$ (non-election panel of Table 3); the stored exact shares in the cell ($d = 0.1$, 95%) are $\tfrac{15/4}{36} = \tfrac{5}{48}$ and $\tfrac{11/4}{10} = \tfrac{11}{40}$. Changing this study's indicator from $1$ to $0$ gives $$\frac{15/4 - 1}{36} = \frac{11}{144} = 0.0763\ldots, \qquad \frac{11/4 - 1}{10} = \frac{7}{40} = 0.175,$$ so Table 2's $0.10$ becomes $0.08$ and Table 3's $0.28$ becomes about $0.18$. Whether the study still reaches 60% and 80% power at $d = 0.1$ is not determined by the cleaned data ((iii): it would need $\sigma \ge 0.343$ and $\sigma \ge 0.434$).
(v) [What survives] For every $\sigma > 0$, estimate $\hat\beta$ and standard error $\mathrm{SE} > 0$: $\dfrac{|\hat\beta|/\sigma}{\mathrm{SE}/\sigma} = \dfrac{|\hat\beta|}{\mathrm{SE}}$. So the study's $t$-statistic and its side of the significance line in Figure 4 do not depend on the standardizing quantity; only its position along the axes does.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed:
From the paper. p. 9 (PDF p. 9): “We measure effect size by Cohen’s $d$, which is the treatment effect standardized by the standard deviation of the outcome (Cohen, 1988). We use the standard deviation of the outcome of control units within the default bandwidth in the rdrobust package for this standardization. We investigate the effect sizes 0.1, 0.2, 0.5 and 0.8.” The power of each analysis is that of “a two-tailed test at the 5% significance level based on a central limit approximation for the sampling distribution” (S6); in the notation of (S7) it is $f(|\tau|/s)$ with $\tau = d \cdot \mathrm{SD}$ and $s$ the bias-corrected robust standard error.
Not in the paper (read by the validator from the deposited files): for Coppock and Green (2016) the reanalysis is a fuzzy RD whose outcome and treatment variables are cell-level counts of voters (the numbers of people in a cell who voted in 2010 and in 2008), the estimated effect is the ratio of the two discontinuities (a per-person probability of voting), and the standardizing quantity is the sample standard deviation of the outcome counts on the left of the cutoff within the bandwidth (24.57954623), so that ‘$d = 0.1$’ is an effect of 2.458 on a probability; the stored bias-corrected robust standard error is $s = 0.0154987506828555$ and the stored power is $1$ at all four effect sizes. [Wald ratio] With cell means of the outcome $\bar Y_E$, $\bar Y_I$ and of the treatment $\bar D_E$, $\bar D_I$ on the two sides of the cutoff, the fuzzy effect is $(\bar Y_E - \bar Y_I)/(\bar D_E - \bar D_I)$. [Sample variance] $\frac{1}{k-1}\sum_{j=1}^k (v_j - \bar v)^2$.
canonical_claim.note: Individual binary-outcome Cohen’s-d comparisons require an individual baseline SD. Preserve the conditional fixed-stored-SE normal-power bound, binary-SD bound, t-ratio invariance and separate table arithmetic; do not treat aggregate-target power 1 as an arithmetic error.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: p. 5: ‘a binomial distribution with equal success probability, capturing that we would expect a study to be equally likely to be just above and below the threshold under the null’, read as the claim that when the 1.96 threshold is irrelevant to publication a study inside a caliper is above the threshold with probability one half; the witnesses are the validators' constructions and are not in the paper
canonical_claim.location: p. 5 (PDF p. 5), left column and the continuation under Table 1; Table 1
canonical_claim.statement:
Exact counterexamples (the validators' constructions; not in the paper): populations of independent studies that are all published whatever their $t$-statistic, so that the 1.96 threshold is irrelevant to publication, in which a study inside a caliper is above the threshold with probability different from $\tfrac12$, and in which the paper's nominal 5% caliper test rejects with conditional probability above 5%. Notation as in definitions_needed; $h = c\,r$ with $c = \tfrac{49}{25}$ and $r \in \{\tfrac{1}{10}, \tfrac{3}{20}, \tfrac15\}$ (the printed 0.196, 0.294, 0.392).
(i) [A linear density] Let $f(x) = x/8$ for $0 \le x \le 4$ and $f(x) = 0$ otherwise; $\int_0^4 x/8\,dx = 1$, and $f$ is positive and smooth on every caliper. Then $A_h = \tfrac{2ch + h^2}{16}$, $B_h = \tfrac{2ch - h^2}{16}$ and $$p_h = \frac12 + \frac{h}{4c} = \frac12 + \frac r4 : \qquad p_h = \tfrac{21}{40},\ \tfrac{43}{80},\ \tfrac{11}{20} \quad\text{for } r = \tfrac{1}{10},\ \tfrac{3}{20},\ \tfrac15 .$$ The three windows are $[\tfrac{441}{250}, \tfrac{539}{250}]$, $[\tfrac{833}{500}, \tfrac{1127}{500}]$ and $[\tfrac{196}{125}, \tfrac{294}{125}]$; for the last, $A_h = \tfrac{26411}{250000}$ and $B_h = \tfrac{21609}{250000}$.
(ii) [The tails at the counts of Table 1] $G_{12,9}(\tfrac12) = \tfrac{299}{4096} = 0.07299\ldots$ and $G_{12,9}(\tfrac{21}{40}) = \tfrac{336637329302285487}{3355443200000000000} = 0.10032\ldots$; $G_{15,11}(\tfrac12) = \tfrac{1941}{32768} = 0.05923\ldots$ and $G_{15,11}(\tfrac{43}{80}) = \tfrac{3589476431322242287677900507}{35184372088832000000000000000} = 0.10201\ldots$; $G_{19,14}(\tfrac12) = \tfrac{2083}{65536} = 0.03178\ldots$ and $$G_{19,14}(\tfrac{11}{20}) = \frac{50930691593528557166389}{655360000000000000000000} = 0.07771\ldots > \frac{1}{20} .$$
(iii) [The nominal 5% test over-rejects] $G_{19,13}(\tfrac12) = \tfrac{10949}{131072} > \tfrac{1}{20} > G_{19,14}(\tfrac12)$, so with 19 studies in the window the test that rejects when the equal-probability tail is at most 5% rejects exactly when $K \ge 14$. In the population of (i), conditional on $N = 19$ in the 20% window, its rejection probability is $G_{19,14}(\tfrac{11}{20}) > \tfrac{1}{20}$.
(iv) [Smoothness gives no bound at a fixed width] For $m = 1, 2, \dots$ let $f_m(x) = (m+1)x^m/4^{m+1}$ on $[0,4]$ and $0$ otherwise. Each $f_m$ is a density, smooth and positive on every caliper, and for $0 < h < c$ $$p_h = \frac{(c+h)^{m+1} - c^{m+1}}{(c+h)^{m+1} - (c-h)^{m+1}} \longrightarrow 1 \quad (m \to \infty) .$$ At $m = 9$ and $h = \tfrac{49}{125}$: $p_h = \tfrac{4609141}{5401600} = 0.8532\ldots$
(v) [With exactly valid inference in every study] Let every study have an estimate $\hat\theta \sim N(\theta, 1)$ with standard error $1$ and $t$-statistic $T = \hat\theta$, let $\theta = \tfrac72$ in every study, and let every study be published; $X = |T|$ has distribution function $F(x) = \Phi(x - \tfrac72) - \Phi(-x - \tfrac72)$, $x \ge 0$. For the 20% window, $p_h = \tfrac{F(c+h) - F(c)}{F(c+h) - F(c-h)}$ satisfies $$0.644747758104 \le p_h \le 0.644747758105, \qquad 0.280413461677 \le G_{19,14}(p_h) \le 0.280413461678 .$$ With $\theta = 0$ in every study instead, $0.318944499071 \le p_h \le 0.318944499072$, below $\tfrac12$ (the departure from $\tfrac12$ can go in either direction).
canonical_claim.definitions_needed:
From the paper. The caliper test and its null, p. 5 (PDF p. 5): quoted in full in the statement of P033-T8. The statistics are the 45 main reported results, one per article, in absolute value (S4). Windows: radii 10%, 15% and 20% of the threshold, “here corresponding to 0.196, 0.294, and 0.392”, around 1.96. The test: “a binomial distribution with equal success probability”, “one-tailed”. The paper gives no condition on the distribution of the $t$-statistics in the absence of selection beyond the null itself (“the 5% significance level is irrelevant for researchers’ and editors’ publication decisions”; “no real pathologies in the RD literature”).
Not in the paper (the validators' formalization): the absolute $t$-statistics of the studies, before any selection, are independent draws $X_1, \dots, X_M$ from a density $f$ on $[0, \infty)$, and under the null every study is published, so the published statistics are those draws. $c = \tfrac{49}{25}$; for a half-width $0 < h < c$, $W_h = [c-h, c+h]$, $$A_h = \int_c^{c+h} f(x)\,dx, \qquad B_h = \int_{c-h}^{c} f(x)\,dx, \qquad p_h = \frac{A_h}{A_h + B_h} \quad (A_h + B_h > 0),$$ $N$ is the number of draws in $W_h$ and $K$ the number in $[c, c+h]$. $G_{n,k}(p)$ is the binomial upper tail of (S7); the paper's $p$-value for $k$ of $n$ studies above the threshold is $G_{n,k}(\tfrac12)$.
canonical_claim.note: P033-N004 is rated an error, Minor (ratings.json; second rating borderline Minor/Moderate), so no printed-statement target is listed. Verdict confirmed in part by two validators (exact counterexample). What is confirmed is a missing condition: the equal-probability benchmark does not follow from the absence of selection alone. Not established, and not asserted: any error in Table 1's counts or binomial arithmetic (they reproduce), the actual density of unselected statistics, a replacement $p$-value for the 45 studies, or a change in the paper's qualitative conclusion. The counter-models are not fitted to the observed histogram. The paper's first paragraph says ‘approximately the same number’, which is right as a shrinking-window statement (P033-T8 (v)); the witnesses address the finite windows actually used. (i)–(iii) are section 3 of both validators' derivations, (iv) is section 4 of runs/P033/validate/P033-N004/v2/artifact/derivation.md, and (v) is section 4 of the first validator's derivation.md, whose check.py certifies the decimal enclosures with rational Taylor bounds. Also bears on P033-H3 (the same test is used in Supplement Tables S4 and S5). The rational values in (i)–(iv) were recomputed for this list with exact arithmetic and the enclosures in (v) at 40 digits.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: The null of the caliper test (p. 5) and the reading of the p-values of Table 1, as repaired by Sol: the binomial tails are computed under a working null of equal probability mass on the two sides of 1.96 inside each caliper, which the absence of selection does not imply (formal content: the exact conditional law of the count, and conditions under which the benchmark is exact, conservative, or approximately right)
canonical_claim.location: p. 5 (PDF p. 5), left column and the continuation under Table 1; Table 1
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed; p. 5] “The test compares the number of studies just above and just below the 1.96 threshold that corresponds to statistical significance at the 5% level. Under the assumption (null hypothesis) that the 5% significance level is irrelevant for researchers’ and editors’ publication decisions, the 1.96 threshold should be immaterial, and we would expect approximately the same number of studies just above and just below it. However, the 1.96 threshold becomes relevant for the publication decision if there is p-hacking or publication bias. In this case, we would not be surprised to see more studies just above the threshold. Following Gerber and Malhotra (2008a, 2008b), we include studies within windows around the cutoff with radii (i.e., half-widths or calipers) of 10%, 15%, and 20% of the threshold itself, here corresponding to 0.196, 0.294, and 0.392, respectively. A smaller window is better targeted towards the 1.96 threshold, but has lower power.” “Table 1 presents the results from the caliper tests. For all three window sizes, there are approximately three times as many studies just above the threshold than just below it. We calculate the probability of observing an imbalance at least this extreme under the null hypothesis of no real pathologies in the RD literature by using a binomial distribution with equal success probability, capturing that we would expect a study to be equally likely to be just above and below the threshold under the null. Following Gerber and Malhotra (2008a, 2008b), the test is one-tailed, reflecting the fact that we feel comfortable ruling out, before seeing the data, that researchers or editors actively favor insignificant findings. The $p$-values of the caliper tests range between 3% and 7%, depending on the window size, indicating that it is unlikely that we would observe this large of an imbalance in the $t$-statistics if there were no real pathologies in the RD literature.” [Printed; Table 1, p. 5, “Caliper tests of imbalance of $t$-statistic among RD studies.”; columns Window, % | Below | Above | $p$-value] 10 | 3 | 9 | 0.073. 15 | 4 | 11 | 0.059. 20 | 5 | 14 | 0.032.
[Corrected; Sol's smallest_repair (validated.json, P033-N004), verbatim] “Identify the actual statistical benchmark and qualify its substantive interpretation: 'Conditional on the number of studies in each caliper, we calculate one-sided binomial tail probabilities under a working null of equal probability mass above and below the threshold. Interpreting these probabilities as evidence of publication bias requires an additional justification that the unselected distribution has approximately equal mass on the two sides, or a sensitivity analysis allowing unequal mass. Publication independence alone does not imply the working null.' Retain Table 1's counts and numbers.” [The second validator's wording of the same repair, verbatim] “Retain the counts and numbers but qualify both caliper paragraphs: 'We use an equal-probability benchmark within each caliper window. Under this benchmark, the one-sided binomial tail probabilities range from 3% to 7%. Interpreting them as calibrated tests of reporting or publication selection additionally requires approximately equal unselected probability mass on the two sides of each window; absence of selection alone does not imply that condition.' Apply the same qualification to the supplementary caliper tests and their null interpretations.”
[Mathematical content, with every hypothesis] Setting and notation as in definitions_needed: $X_1, \dots, X_M$ independent with density $f$, all published; $0 < h < c$; $A_h + B_h > 0$.
(i) [The exact conditional law] For every $n$ with $P(N = n) > 0$, conditionally on $N = n$ the count $K$ of statistics above the threshold has the Binomial$(n, p_h)$ distribution; in particular $P(K \ge k \mid N = n) = G_{n,k}(p_h)$.
(ii) [When the benchmark is exact] $p_h = \tfrac12$ if and only if $A_h = B_h$. A sufficient condition is local symmetry, $f(c + u) = f(c - u)$ for $0 < u < h$; in particular a density that is constant on $W_h$.
(iii) [When the one-sided test is conservative] $G_{n,k}(p)$ is nondecreasing in $p$ for all $0 \le k \le n$. If $f$ is nonincreasing on $W_h$, then $A_h \le B_h$, $p_h \le \tfrac12$ and $G_{n,k}(p_h) \le G_{n,k}(\tfrac12)$: the paper's tail probability is then an upper bound on the true one. If $f$ is nondecreasing on $W_h$, the inequalities are reversed.
(iv) [A quantitative bound at a fixed width] If $f(x) \ge a > 0$ for $x \in W_h$ and $|f(x) - f(y)| \le L|x - y|$ for $x, y \in W_h$, then $|A_h - B_h| \le L h^2$, $A_h + B_h \ge 2ha$ and $$\Big|p_h - \frac12\Big| = \frac{|A_h - B_h|}{2(A_h + B_h)} \le \frac{L h}{4a} .$$
(v) [The sense in which ‘approximately the same number’ holds] If $f$ is continuous at $c$ and $f(c) > 0$, then $p_h \to \tfrac12$ as $h \downarrow 0$. If moreover $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then $p_h - \tfrac12 = \dfrac{h f'(c)}{4 f(c)} + o(h)$. Neither statement bounds $|p_h - \tfrac12|$ at $h = 0.196$, $0.294$ or $0.392$ (P033-T7 (iv)).
(vi) [The printed numbers are the benchmark's tails] $G_{12,9}(\tfrac12) = \tfrac{299}{4096}$, $G_{15,11}(\tfrac12) = \tfrac{1941}{32768}$ and $G_{19,14}(\tfrac12) = \tfrac{2083}{65536}$, which round to the printed 0.073, 0.059 and 0.032.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed:
From the paper. The caliper test and its null, p. 5 (PDF p. 5): quoted in full in the statement of P033-T8. The statistics are the 45 main reported results, one per article, in absolute value (S4). Windows: radii 10%, 15% and 20% of the threshold, “here corresponding to 0.196, 0.294, and 0.392”, around 1.96. The test: “a binomial distribution with equal success probability”, “one-tailed”. The paper gives no condition on the distribution of the $t$-statistics in the absence of selection beyond the null itself (“the 5% significance level is irrelevant for researchers’ and editors’ publication decisions”; “no real pathologies in the RD literature”).
Not in the paper (the validators' formalization): the absolute $t$-statistics of the studies, before any selection, are independent draws $X_1, \dots, X_M$ from a density $f$ on $[0, \infty)$, and under the null every study is published, so the published statistics are those draws. $c = \tfrac{49}{25}$; for a half-width $0 < h < c$, $W_h = [c-h, c+h]$, $$A_h = \int_c^{c+h} f(x)\,dx, \qquad B_h = \int_{c-h}^{c} f(x)\,dx, \qquad p_h = \frac{A_h}{A_h + B_h} \quad (A_h + B_h > 0),$$ $N$ is the number of draws in $W_h$ and $K$ the number in $[c, c+h]$. $G_{n,k}(p)$ is the binomial upper tail of (S7); the paper's $p$-value for $k$ of $n$ studies above the threshold is $G_{n,k}(\tfrac12)$.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: Part (v) is a limit as the half-width tends to zero; the finite statements behind it are the identity $p_h - \tfrac12 = (A_h - B_h)/[2(A_h + B_h)]$ and the bound of (iv). Parts (i)–(iv) and (vi) are exact for each fixed $h$.
canonical_claim.note: Priority 3 (Minor). The repair is a weaker reading of the same numbers: Table 1's counts and tails stand, as tails under an equal-mass working null. (i)–(ii) are section 2 of both validators' derivations; (iii) and (iv) are section 5 of the first validator's derivation.md and section 4 of the second's (runs/P033/validate/P033-N004/v2/artifact/derivation.md); (v) is section 5 of the first; (vi) is their reproduction of Table 1. In (i) the number $M$ of studies is fixed and the conditioning is on the count in the window only; the paper's 45 studies and its windows give $n = 12$, $15$, $19$. Nothing here estimates $p_h$ for the surveyed literature: its size and direction are not established. The same qualification applies to the caliper tests of Supplement Tables S4 and S5 (P033-H3).

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Power analysis, p. 9: ‘The power analyses presume that p-values will be constructed with the bias adjustment and robust standard errors as implemented by rdrobust’, with Tables 2 and 3, corrected for four clustered estimates whose saved power uses a standard error smaller than the fitted robust one (formal content: the normal power function, its strict monotonicity, the cluster-count factor, and the arithmetic of the six affected cells)
canonical_claim.location: p. 9 (PDF p. 9), Power analysis, left column, and Table 2; Table 3, p. 10 (PDF p. 10), ‘Studies using election data’
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed; p. 9] “Using the power analysis method implemented in the R package rdpower by Cattaneo et al. (2019), we estimate the power of a two-tailed test at the 5% significance level based on a central limit approximation for the sampling distribution. The power analyses presume that $p$-values will be constructed with the bias adjustment and robust standard errors as implemented by rdrobust.” [Printed; Table 2, p. 9; rows 0.5 and 0.8, columns 60 | 80 | 95] 0.5: 0.65 | 0.56 | 0.48. 0.8: 0.78 | 0.70 | 0.65. [Printed; Table 3, p. 10, ‘Studies using election data’] 0.5: 0.59 | 0.46 | 0.40. 0.8: 0.78 | 0.66 | 0.59.
[Corrected; Sol's smallest_repair (validated.json, P033-E010), verbatim] “For the four verified estimates, replace the saved powers by Phi(|d*SD_control|/SE_native-z_0.975)+Phi(-|d*SD_control|/SE_native-z_0.975), using the same fitted robust SE as the declared test and preserving effect standardization, bandwidths, and study weights. Reaggregate Tables 2–3. The same current-design repair rule can be applied to other estimates once their native fitted variances are verified; the complete earlier replacement tables are not certified here.” [Corrected text; validated.json, prior_correction.corrected_text, verbatim] “In four independently checked sharp clustered-RD estimates (Gerber/Hopkins, Hall/Thompson, Lopes de Fonseca, and Sances), saved retrospective powers use a smaller SE consistent with the factor sqrt(G/(G_L+G_R)) instead of the native fitted robust SE. Holding effects, bandwidths, weights, and all other estimates fixed, native-SE replacement changes Table 2 entries (d,power threshold) (0.5,.60), (0.8,.60), (0.8,.95) to .62, .76, .62 and the corresponding Table 3 election entries to .55, .74, .55. This is a verified partial repair. The earlier full corrected tables and ten-estimate count remain unverified because the additional data and original package are unavailable. The repair preserves the fitted variance approximation and does not establish its validity for arbitrary cluster covariance or future designs.”
[Mathematical content, with every hypothesis] $z = \Phi^{-1}(39/40)$; $f(a) = \Phi(a - z) + \Phi(-a - z)$ for $a \ge 0$, as in (S7).
(i) [The power the text describes] If the test statistic is distributed $N(\tau/s, 1)$, with $s > 0$ the fitted bias-corrected robust standard error and $\tau$ the hypothesized effect, then the two-tailed test that rejects when the absolute statistic exceeds $z$ has rejection probability $$P\big(|N(\tau/s, 1)| > z\big) = \Phi(|\tau|/s - z) + \Phi(-|\tau|/s - z) = f(|\tau|/s),$$ and $f(0) = \tfrac{1}{20}$. With Cohen's $d$ and the control standard deviation $\sigma_0$ of (S6), $\tau = d\,\sigma_0$.
(ii) [Strict monotonicity] $f'(a) = \varphi(a - z) - \varphi(a + z) > 0$ for $a > 0$, because $(a + z)^2 - (a - z)^2 = 4az > 0$. Hence $f$ is strictly increasing on $[0, \infty)$, and a value $f(a) \in (\tfrac{1}{20}, 1)$ determines $a$.
(iii) [The cluster-count factor] Let $\mathcal{L}$ and $\mathcal{R}$ be the finite nonempty sets of cluster labels that occur on the left and on the right of the cutoff, $G_L = |\mathcal{L}|$, $G_R = |\mathcal{R}|$ and $G = |\mathcal{L} \cup \mathcal{R}|$. Then $G_L + G_R = G + |\mathcal{L} \cap \mathcal{R}|$, so $$\frac12 \le \rho := \frac{G}{G_L + G_R} \le 1, \qquad \rho < 1 \iff \mathcal{L} \cap \mathcal{R} \ne \emptyset .$$
(iv) [A smaller standard error overstates power] For $\tau \ne 0$, $s > 0$ and $0 < \rho < 1$: $f\big(|\tau|/(s\sqrt{\rho})\big) > f(|\tau|/s)$. Premise from the deposited results: for four clustered estimates the saved powers equal $f(|\tau|/(s\sqrt\rho))$ with $\rho = G/(G_L + G_R)$ and differ from $f(|\tau|/s)$; their counts $(G, G_L, G_R)$ are $(57, 23, 46)$ for Gerber and Hopkins (2011), $(185, 98, 101)$ for Hall and Thompson (2018), $(278, 202, 226)$ for Lopes da Fonseca (2017) and $(204, 133, 130)$ for Sances (2017), which give overlaps $12$, $14$, $150$, $59$ and $$\rho = \tfrac{19}{23},\quad \tfrac{185}{199},\quad \tfrac{139}{214},\quad \tfrac{204}{263},$$ each strictly less than $1$. So each of their sixteen saved powers is strictly larger than the power of the test the text describes.
(v) [Arithmetic of the six affected cells; premises from the deposited results] Premises: total weight $36$ in Table 2 and $26$ in the election panel of Table 3; Lopes da Fonseca and Sances are election studies of weight $1$; with the fitted standard error, Lopes da Fonseca's power falls below $0.60$ at $d = 0.5$ (saved 0.7738, corrected 0.5891) and below $0.95$ at $d = 0.8$ (0.9913, 0.9378), and Sances's falls below $0.60$ at $d = 0.8$ (0.6629, 0.5543); no other threshold is crossed. Then, in Table 2, $$\tfrac{31}{48} - \tfrac{1}{36} = \tfrac{89}{144}, \qquad \tfrac{113}{144} - \tfrac{1}{36} = \tfrac{109}{144}, \qquad \tfrac{31}{48} - \tfrac{1}{36} = \tfrac{89}{144}$$ for the cells $(d, \text{threshold}) = (0.5, 60)$, $(0.8, 60)$, $(0.8, 95)$: the printed 0.65, 0.78, 0.65 become 0.62, 0.76, 0.62; and in the election panel of Table 3, $$\tfrac{61}{104} - \tfrac{1}{26} = \tfrac{57}{104}, \qquad \tfrac{81}{104} - \tfrac{1}{26} = \tfrac{77}{104}, \qquad \tfrac{61}{104} - \tfrac{1}{26} = \tfrac{57}{104}$$ for the same three cells: the printed 0.59, 0.78, 0.59 become 0.55, 0.74, 0.55.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed:
From the paper: standing assumption (S6) (the two-tailed 5% test, the central limit approximation, the bias adjustment and robust standard errors of rdrobust, Cohen's $d$ and its standardization, the weighting of Table 2). The paper prints no formula for the power; $f$ is the normal-approximation power that its description determines (the first validator: the text describes ‘approximate powers for the bias-corrected rdrobust test’; an independent reader found the stored powers equal to this formula for every non-clustered staged estimate).
Not in the paper (read by the validators from the deposited results and data): the saved powers of four clustered estimates match $f(|\tau|/(s\sqrt{G/(G_L + G_R)}))$ to within $10^{-15}$, with $G$, $G_L$, $G_R$ the numbers of distinct clusters among complete cases overall, left and right of the cutoff; the exact statements of the rdpower source that produce the factor were not available to the validators. The weights of Tables 2 and 3 are the reciprocals of the number of analyses per article.
canonical_claim.note: P033-E010 is rated an error, Minor (ratings.json). It is a numerical disagreement between the saved powers and the calculation the text describes, not a false printed formula; it is on the list because its correction is a formula (the standard error that enters the normal power function) with exact formal content, (ii)–(iv), that bears on printed cells. The validators gave no counterexample (evidence type: recalculation from source), so there is no counterexample target. Verdict confirmed in part by two validators: four estimates and six cells are verified; the earlier claim of ten estimates and twelve cells could not be checked for want of data and is not part of this target. The correction lowers power and leaves the percentages quoted in the text for 80% power (22%, 56%, 70%) unchanged. (i)–(ii) are section 1, (iii)–(iv) section 3 and (v) section 5 of the first validator's derivation.md; the second validator's is runs/P033/validate/P033-E010/v2/artifact/derivation.md. The decimal powers quoted in (v) are the validators' 80-digit evaluations and are premises; the fractions were recomputed for this list with exact arithmetic. The repair keeps the fitted variance and does not certify it (see P033-T3 and P033-T4 for a separate defect of the clustered variance). Also bears on P033-H6.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: p. 7: ‘The boundary for statistical significance at the 5% level is a line emanating from the origin with a slope of 1.96 […] where estimates to the right of this line attain statistical significance’, and ‘We use the sample variance of the outcome among control units for the standardization’, as printed; the witnesses are the validator's and are not in the paper
canonical_claim.location: p. 7 (PDF p. 7), Results, right column, paragraph beginning ‘We can disaggregate the information in Figure 3’; Figure 4, p. 8 (PDF p. 8)
canonical_claim.statement:
Exact witnesses (the validator's; not in the paper) against the printed slope of the significance line and against the printed name of the standardizing quantity. Coordinates as in definitions_needed: horizontal $x = |\hat\beta|/s_0$, vertical $y = \mathrm{SE}/s_0$, with $s_0 > 0$.
(i) [The printed slope misclassifies] Take $x = y = \tfrac12$, a point inside the plotted ranges $0 \le x \le 2$, $0 \le y \le 0.8$. Its $t$-statistic is $|t| = x/y = 1 < \tfrac{49}{25}$, so it is not significant at the 5% level. The line through the origin with slope $\tfrac{49}{25}$, $y = \tfrac{49}{25}x$, reaches the height $y = \tfrac12$ at $x = \tfrac{25}{98}$, and $\tfrac12 > \tfrac{25}{98}$: the point lies to the right of that line. So the printed description (slope 1.96, estimates to the right of the line significant) classifies this nonsignificant estimate as significant. On the line with the reciprocal slope, $y = \tfrac{25}{49}x$, the height at $x = \tfrac12$ is $\tfrac{25}{98} < \tfrac12$, and the point lies above that line, on its nonsignificant side.
(ii) [Variance and standard deviation are different divisors] The control outcomes $(0, 2, 4)$ have mean $2$, sample variance $\tfrac{(0-2)^2 + (2-2)^2 + (4-2)^2}{3-1} = 4$ and sample standard deviation $2$. For an estimate $1$ with standard error $\tfrac12$, dividing by the standard deviation gives the point $(\tfrac12, \tfrac14)$ and dividing by the variance gives $(\tfrac14, \tfrac18)$: two different points, with the same ratio $x/y = 2$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed:
From the paper. p. 7 (PDF p. 7): “We can disaggregate the information in Figure 3 using a funnel plot, which is a scatter plot with standardized point estimates and standardized estimated standard errors on the two axes. Figure 4 presents such a funnel plot for the 39 estimates in the replication study.$^{3}$ We use the sample variance of the outcome among control units for the standardization. The boundary for statistical significance at the 5% level is a line emanating from the origin with a slope of 1.96, here drawn in red, where estimates to the right of this line attain statistical significance at the conventional level.” Figure 4, p. 8 (PDF p. 8): in each panel the horizontal axis is labelled ‘Point estimate’ (ticks 0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0), the vertical axis ‘Standard error’ (ticks 0.0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8), and the red line through the origin is labelled ‘t = 1.96’. p. 8: “We note that the estimates cluster around the red line corresponding to a $t$-statistic of 1.96, especially in the first panel.”
Not in the paper (read by the validator from the deposited plotting script): the plotted coordinates are $x = |\hat\beta|/s_0$ and $y = \mathrm{SE}/s_0$, where $s_0$ is the sample standard deviation of the outcome among observations below the cutoff, and the red line is drawn with slope $1/\Phi^{-1}(0.975)$. The $t$-statistic of a plotted estimate is $|t| = |\hat\beta|/\mathrm{SE}$; ‘slope’ means the coefficient $k$ in the equation $y = kx$ of the line in the plotted coordinates.
canonical_claim.note: P033-E003 is rated an error, Minor (ratings.json): two slips of wording on p. 7, a reciprocal constant and a wrong name for the divisor. The figure, its label ‘t = 1.96’ and the code are right, and no number changes. Sol's verdict is confirmed (upheld on re-run), evidence type Lean proof: the validator's own file runs/P033/validate/P033-E003/v1/artifact/check.lean already proves (i) as `printed_line_counterexample` and the arithmetic of (ii) as `sample_variance_example`, `sample_sd_example` and `normalization_example`; the formalizer should state these in the present project's conventions and need not reuse that file. The sentence ‘We use the sample variance … for the standardization’ does not literally say ‘divide by the variance’; (ii) shows only that the two readings give different coordinates. The finding relates to the funnel plot of P033-H2.
